title: Polynomial-time minimum-total-length disjoint paths for fixed k
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an undirected unweighted graph G and k prescribed terminal pairs \((s_{i},t_{i})\), outputs pairwise vertex-disjoint paths \(\mathrm{P}_{i}\) from \(s_{i}\) to \(t_{i}\) minimizing \(\sum _{i}|E(\mathrm{P}_{i})|\), or correctly reports that no such collection exists? Randomized algorithms with success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input are admitted in this reading, consistently with the randomized \(k=2\) baseline cited by the source. Polynomial degree and constants may depend on k; an FPT bound with exponent independent of k is not requested.
context:
Disjointness can force one route away from its own shortest path. The optimization problem allows such detours and asks for the smallest total number of edges over all routes. An algorithm checking only whether all individual shortest distances can be attained cannot handle the remaining instances.

The source gives polynomial-time algorithms for individually shortest paths at every fixed k and cites a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for minimum total length when \(k=2\). It leaves the minimum-total-length extension open for \(k\ge 3\).

The 2024 grid result handles minimum-total-length routing on an infinite rectangular grid. Its geometric restriction does not give the requested algorithm on arbitrary undirected graphs.

The 2025 planar preprint requires every route to be individually shortest. That condition does not handle general minimum-total-length routing when disjointness forces detours.

The published 2025 cycle-packing paper explicitly states that Min-Sum Disjoint Paths remains open even for three pairs on planar graphs. Its own polynomial-time result packs cycles without prescribed terminal pairs, so it does not settle this routing problem.
why: Would determine whether exact length optimization preserves the polynomial-time solvability of undirected disjoint routing with a fixed number of prescribed terminal pairs.
status_note: Checked the original graph model and concluding question, the full 2025 cycle-packing discussion, and the exact scopes of the 2024 grid and 2025 planar results. Searches through 12 September 2026 identified no general fixed-k polynomial-time algorithm. Randomized bounded-error solvability is explicitly admitted as in the source’\(s k=2\) comparison.

references.title: Using a Geometric Lens to Find k Disjoint Shortest Paths
references.authors: Bentert, Matthias; Nichterlein, André; Renken, Malte; Zschoche, Philipp
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 13; PDF page 13

definitions: G is a finite simple connected undirected graph with n numbered vertices and unit length on every edge, encoded by an adjacency matrix and the terminal labels. Take the 2k terminals to be distinct; repeated endpoints across different pairs make vertex-disjointness infeasible, and a pair with \(s_{i}=t_{i}\) uses the zero-edge path at that vertex and can be handled separately. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent. Vertex-disjointness includes endpoints and means \(V(\mathrm{P}_{i})\cap V(\mathrm{P}_{j})=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Pairings are fixed: connecting a source to a different pair’s target is not acceptable. Define OPT as the minimum sum of edge counts over all feasible collections and set OPT=∞ when there is none. The output consists of the k vertex sequences of an optimal collection, or an infeasibility answer. For each fixed k the algorithm is a probabilistic Turing machine, with one finite program handling all n and all inputs for that k, running in at most \(C_{k}(n+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps on every random-bit sequence. Constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\) are independent of n. With probability at least \(2/3\) over its independent fair bits, the full output must be correct, including exact optimality. A deterministic algorithm is included as the zero-error case. The formulation asks for polynomial time for each fixed k and does not demand a uniform procedure generating these programs as k varies. The source compares this target with k-DSP, which requires every \(\mathrm{P}_{i}\) separately to have length \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s_{i},t_{i})\). Such a collection, when it exists, has the smallest possible total length; minimum-total-length routing must also handle inputs where disjoint routes exist but no collection of individually shortest routes exists.
answer_criterion: Establish or refute polynomial-time solvability, with the stated bounded-error allowance, for every fixed \(k\ge 3\). A positive answer must output an exactly optimal collection or detect infeasibility on all inputs. A conditional negative answer must state its assumption and imply that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists for at least one fixed k. Hardness only when k grows with n, an FPT lower bound, approximation, or an algorithm restricted to individually shortest paths does not decide this question.
